cards.back: Discrete subunit of a cell adapted to a specific function, e.g. nucleus, ribosome, vesicle, plasma membrane. Not organelles: cell wall, cytoskeleton, cytoplasm.

cards.front: Are ribosomes organelles even though they have no membrane?
cards.back: Yes. An organelle is a discrete functional subunit; a membrane is not required.
Breaking cells open and separating organelles by (ultra)centrifugation, so each type can be studied alone. An example of a new technique driving progress.

cards.front: Why separate the nucleus from the cytoplasm?
cards.back: Transcription and translation are kept apart, so mRNA can be processed (modified) before it reaches ribosomes.

cards.front: Prokaryotes vs eukaryotes: when can translation start?
cards.back: Prokaryotes have no nucleus, so ribosomes can begin translating mRNA while it is still being transcribed. In eukaryotes mRNA is processed first and leaves through nuclear pores.

cards.front: Advantages of compartments in the cytoplasm
cards.back: Enzymes and substrates are concentrated in one place, and incompatible processes are kept apart.
They hold digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes that would damage the cell if free. Phagocytic vacuoles fuse with lysosomes to digest what was engulfed.

cards.front: AHL: How is the mitochondrion adapted for ATP production?
cards.back: Double membrane with a small intermembrane space (proton gradient builds quickly); cristae give a large inner-membrane area for electron transport chains and ATP synthase; matrix holds Krebs cycle enzymes.

cards.front: AHL: How is the chloroplast adapted for photosynthesis?
cards.back: Large thylakoid membrane area holding photosystems; small fluid volume inside thylakoids (proton gradient builds fast); stroma holds Calvin cycle enzymes and substrates.
Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane that increase its surface area.

cards.front: AHL: Why does the nucleus have a double membrane with pores?
cards.back: Pores let mRNA out and proteins (e.g. enzymes, histones) in while keeping DNA inside.

cards.front: AHL: What happens to the nuclear membrane in mitosis and meiosis?
cards.back: It breaks into vesicles so spindle microtubules can reach the chromosomes, then re-forms around each new nucleus.

cards.front: AHL: Free ribosomes vs ribosomes on rough ER
cards.back: Free ribosomes: proteins for use in the cytoplasm. Rough-ER ribosomes: proteins that enter the ER for other organelles, the plasma membrane or secretion.

cards.front: AHL: Role of the Golgi apparatus
cards.back: Receives proteins from the rough ER in vesicles, modifies them (e.g. adds carbohydrate) and packages them into vesicles for secretion. It does not make proteins.

cards.front: AHL: Path of a secreted protein
cards.back: Rough-ER ribosome → ER lumen → vesicle → Golgi (modified) → secretory vesicle → fuses with plasma membrane (exocytosis).
Small membrane-bound sac that carries materials within the cell or to the plasma membrane.
Clathrin proteins assemble into a cage-like coat on a patch of membrane, curving it into a pit that pinches off as a vesicle (e.g. in endocytosis).
